A change to a dialplan, a proxy script or a trunk can break calls that nobody
places until a customer does. An expectation suite states what a test call
capture must show: how many calls, what share answered, how many conformance
errors, how good the audio was. `sipnab --expect` judges a capture against it
and exits non-zero when a rule fails, so the step that runs it fails the build.

## What you need

- A sipnab build with the default features. Judging a capture file needs no
  privileges.
- A capture of the traffic you want to judge. In a pipeline that is usually a
  test run: SIPp or a test phone places calls through a staging server while
  sipnab or `tcpdump` records them.
- A suite file in your repository, `sipnab.expect.toml` by convention.
- No change on any other system. The suite reads the capture only, so nothing
  on your SIP servers changes.

## Write a suite

A suite is a list of rules. Each rule measures one figure over the capture's
calls and compares it with a threshold:

```toml
[[rules]]
name = "calls captured"
metric = "count"
op = ">="
value = 5

[[rules]]
name = "answer-seizure ratio"
metric = "asr"
op = ">="
value = 50

[[rules]]
name = "no busy answers"
metric = "count"
op = "=="
value = 0
scope = "filter:response_code == 486"
```

This is [`tests/fixtures/expect/sip-problem-call.expect.toml`](https://github.com/NormB/sipnab/blob/main/tests/fixtures/expect/sip-problem-call.expect.toml) in a source
checkout.

| Key | Required | What it takes |
|---|---|---|
| `metric` | yes | `count`: the calls in scope. `asr`: the percentage of INVITEs with a final response that the far end answered. `lint_errors`: the conformance findings at or above a severity. `mos_p<N>`: the Nth percentile of the streams' MOS, from `mos_p0` (the worst stream) to `mos_p100` (the best) |
| `op` | yes | `>=`, `>`, `<=`, `<`, `==` or `!=` |
| `value` | yes | The threshold, a number |
| `name` | no | A label for the output. Without it, the output names the rule by its position, such as `#1` |
| `scope` | no | `filter:<expression>` narrows the rule to the calls a [filter](@/docs/filter-dsl.md) selects; an alias such as `filter:problems` works too. `severity:<info, notice, warning or error>` sets the lowest severity a `lint_errors` rule counts. Without it, the rule reads the whole capture |
| `min_sample` | no | The fewest calls (or streams, for MOS) the rule needs. Below it, the rule is `skipped` instead of judged |
| `grounded_only` | no | MOS rules only. `true` (the default) reads only streams whose codec has a published impairment value. `false` admits the others, and the result says so |

An `asr` or MOS rule that measured nothing fails: an `asr` rule whose scope
holds no INVITE with a final response, or a MOS rule over a capture with no
RTP, does not pass by default. Give it `min_sample` when an empty population is
acceptable. A `count` rule always measures something: a scope that selects no
call counts 0, so `count == 0` passes.

## Run it

```sh
sipnab -I tests/pcap-samples/sip-problem-call.pcap --expect tests/fixtures/expect/sip-problem-call.expect.toml --no-cli-print --quiet
```

```text
Expectations: fail, 1 of 3 rules passed, 2 failed
Rule                  Metric  Op  Threshold  Observed  Sample  Verdict
----------------------------------------------------------------------
calls captured        count   >=  5          5         5       pass
answer-seizure ratio  asr     >=  50         20        5       fail
no busy answers       count   ==  0          1         5       fail
answer-seizure ratio: 20 is NOT >= 50 over 5 seizure(s)
no busy answers: 1 is NOT == 0 over 5 dialog(s)
```

The first line is the suite's verdict. Each rule's row gives what it observed
and over how many calls, and each failed rule repeats on a line of its own.

The run exits with the verdict:

| Exit | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `0` | Every rule that ran passed |
| `3` | At least one rule failed |
| `2` | No rule ran, because each one's population was below its `min_sample`. Or sipnab could not read the suite, or the suite holds a rule sipnab refuses |
| `1` | sipnab could not read the capture |

sipnab reads and checks the suite before it reads the capture, so a mistake in
the file stops the run at once.

### Check that it worked

Print the exit status after the run. The sample suite has two failing rules,
so the status is 3:

```sh
sipnab -I tests/pcap-samples/sip-problem-call.pcap --expect tests/fixtures/expect/sip-problem-call.expect.toml --no-cli-print --quiet > /dev/null; echo $?
```

```text
3
```

A status of 3 with the `Expectations: fail` line means the suite ran and
judged the capture. A status of 2 or 1 means it did not judge it:
[When it does not work](#when-it-does-not-work) lists the causes.

The rules judge every call in the capture. `--filter` and `--since` do not
narrow them. Narrow a rule with its own `scope`.

## Run it in a pipeline

Run the suite as its own step, after the step that records the capture. The
step fails when sipnab exits non-zero:

```sh
sipnab -I test-calls.pcap --expect sipnab.expect.toml --no-cli-print --quiet
```

To keep a machine-readable record of the verdict, write the JSON report as
well. `exit_code` is the run's exit status:

```sh
sipnab -I tests/pcap-samples/sip-problem-call.pcap --expect tests/fixtures/expect/sip-problem-call.expect.toml --json --no-cli-print --quiet | jq -c '{verdict, exit_code, failed: [.results[] | select(.verdict == "fail") | .name]}'
```

```json
{"verdict":"fail","exit_code":3,"failed":["answer-seizure ratio","no busy answers"]}
```

A pipe hands the shell `jq`'s exit status, not sipnab's. In a script, read
`exit_code` from the JSON, or use `set -o pipefail`.

## Check conformance in the same suite

A `lint_errors` rule counts the [conformance linter](@/docs/sip-lint-rules.md)'s
findings, so one suite can fail a build on non-conformant SIP as well as on
failed calls. The `scope` sets the lowest severity counted:

```toml
[[rules]]
name = "no conformance errors"
metric = "lint_errors"
op = "=="
value = 0
scope = "severity:error"
```

With that rule in `lint.expect.toml`, against the capture that ships with
sipnab to show what the linter finds:

```sh
sipnab -I tests/pcap-samples/sip-lint-findings.pcap --expect lint.expect.toml --no-cli-print --quiet
```

```text
Expectations: fail, 0 of 1 rule passed, 1 failed
Rule                   Metric       Op  Threshold  Observed  Sample  Verdict
----------------------------------------------------------------------------
no conformance errors  lint_errors  ==  0          2         3       fail
no conformance errors: 2 is NOT == 0 over 3 dialog(s)
```

The rule honors the same suppressions as `--lint`: a `.sipnablint` file beside
the capture, or the file `--lint-suppress-file` names. See
[Suppress a rule](@/docs/sip-lint-rules.md#suppress-a-rule).

## Ask from an agent

The MCP tool `evaluate_expectations` judges the capture the server holds. It
takes the rules inline as JSON, or a suite file's text in `rules_toml`, and
returns the same report. See
[`evaluate_expectations`](@/docs/mcp-tools-security.md#evaluate-expectations).

## When it does not work

A metric sipnab does not know stops the run before it reads the capture, with
exit 2. The message names the suite file you gave, here
`sipnab.expect.toml`, and lists the metrics sipnab takes:

```text
error: invalid value 'sipnab.expect.toml' for '--expect <FILE>': sipnab.expect.toml: rule 0: unknown metric 'asr2'. Known metrics: count, asr, lint_errors, mos_p<N>. A percentile is spelled mos_p10, mos_p50, mos_p90 and so on, from mos_p0 (worst stream) to mos_p100 (best)
```

A rule that measured nothing fails, and says why. Here a MOS rule over
`sip-problem-call.pcap`, which holds no RTP:

```text
Expectations: fail, 0 of 1 rule passed, 1 failed
Rule  Metric   Op  Threshold  Observed  Sample  Verdict
-------------------------------------------------------
#1    mos_p10  >=  3.50       -         0       fail
#1: unevaluable: no scored stream was in scope, so 'mos_p10 >= 3.5' rests on nothing. Declare a min_sample of 1 or more to accept an empty population in writing; a gate does not pass on data it never judged
```

With `min_sample = 1` sipnab skips the same rule instead, and a suite in which
sipnab skipped every rule exits 2:

```text
Expectations: not evaluated, 0 of 0 rules passed, 1 skipped
Rule  Metric   Op  Threshold  Observed  Sample  Verdict
-------------------------------------------------------
#1    mos_p10  >=  3.50       -         0       skipped
#1: skipped: 0 scored stream(s) is below the declared min_sample of 1
```

| What you see | Why | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| Exit 2 before sipnab reads the capture, naming a rule | The suite has a metric, operator, scope or key sipnab does not take, or a filter that does not parse | Fix the rule the message names |
| Exit 2 and `not evaluated` | Every rule was below its `min_sample` | Capture more calls, or lower `min_sample` |
| A rule fails with `unevaluable` and `Sample` 0 | An `asr` or MOS rule measured nothing: its scope held no INVITE with a final response, or no stream | Check the filter with `--report --filter`. Give `min_sample` if an empty capture is acceptable |
| A MOS rule fails on a capture with audio | `grounded_only` excluded streams whose codec has no published impairment value | See [MOS and codecs](@/docs/mos-and-codecs.md), or set `grounded_only = false` and read the caveat |
| The step passes although a rule failed | A pipe returned the exit status of the last command | Run sipnab on its own, or use `set -o pipefail` |
